summary.text: 河 means “river.” The left part, 氵, is the side form of 水, “water,” and identifies the meaning. 可 on the right supplies sound. The character was used especially for the Yellow River in early writing, before its broader use for rivers.

formation.text: A meaning component, 水, is combined with a pronunciation component, now written 可.

components.text: The three strokes are the normal side form of 水. They identify the character as concerning water.
可 supplies sound, not its independent meaning. The familiar form retains this phonetic, although some earlier spellings used other related forms.

sound.text: The modern readings share the final e but differ in initial and tone. The sound clue reflects an older relationship.
Both reconstructed forms contain aːl. The initial consonants differ, and 可 has an additional final glottal stop, ʔ.

history.text: The water element is stable across early spellings, while the sound element varies: oracle forms include 丂 or 何, bronze forms include 𣄰, and Warring States manuscripts have the reduced 可 form also found in seal writing. This is a history of changing phonetic shapes within a water character.

The sound relationship belongs to older Chinese. One reconstruction gives 河 as *ɡaːl and 可 as *kʰaːlʔ: their endings resemble each other despite differences in the initial sound and final consonant. These are reconstructed pronunciations, marked by an asterisk, rather than recordings of ancient speech.

uncertainties.text: The early spellings are more varied than the modern two-part form suggests. Their precise component identifications differ across analyses, so 可 should not be projected unchanged into every early example.
